@@131611689 <p> Raleigh is using AI-enhanced flood forecasting and real-time sensors across city creeks to spot rising water sooner and give crews more time to protect drivers and neighborhoods during heavy storms . <p> Posted 11/20/2025 , 6:25:28 PM <p> Related <p> artificial intelligence <p> flash flood <p> flooding <p> Raleigh <p> A file photo of a car driving through flooded waters . Authorities recommend drivers turn around in this scenario . <p> By Liz McLaughlin , WRAL climate change reporter <p> In mid-August , a sudden burst of heavy rain turned parts of Raleigh 's Capital Boulevard into a torrent . <p> Several vehicles were submerged and motorists were put in danger as water rose faster than emergency crews could respond . Similar scenes played out along Walnut Creek and other low-lying corridors across the city , where brief but intense flash floods have become more common . <p> Other WRAL Top Stories <p> Those events are exactly what Raleigh 's expanding Flood Early Warning System is designed to catch . <p> The system pulls data from rain gauges , stream sensors , radar and soil readings across the city @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ supported by artificial intelligence to help engineers understand which creeks may rise , how quickly water could climb and how much time first responders have before conditions become dangerous . <p> " The system gives emergency responders extra time and helps them know where to focus their efforts , " said Liz Marks , director of product marketing at AEM , the environmental technology firm that provides key rainfall and flood-forecasting data . " Even 30 minutes can make a really big impact . " <h> A flood that arrived too fast <p> Raleigh accelerated its push for better forecasting after 2018 , when a flash flood near Crabtree Valley Mall washed out part of a road before officials realized it was happening . Water rose so quickly that crews could not close the roadway in time . <p> " That was the catalyst , " Marks said . " They realized they needed something better for these flashy creeks . " <h> How the system works <p> The citywide system updates every five minutes , a sharp shift from earlier methods that often refreshed only once an hour . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ creeks can rise violently during short , intense storms . <p> To generate flood predictions , the system combines : <p> real-time stream and rain gauge data <p> radar-adjusted rainfall estimates <p> soil moisture and infiltration readings <p> drainage and watershed information <p> short-term and multi-day rainfall forecasts <p> AEM provides two pieces of the puzzle : highly precise rainfall estimates and a hydrologic model that forecasts how water will move across the city once it falls . <p> " It is designed to continuously recalibrate as storms come in , " Marks said . <h> How forecasts are used <p> Although the system is citywide , Lake Johnson has become one place where crews use forecast information to reduce downstream flood risk . Before major storms , engineers sometimes lower the lake to give rising water somewhere to go . The decision depends on a range of inputs , and the FEWS forecasts are one of them . <p> " Our model can show the expected rise in water level , " Marks said . " City engineers use that information , along with other inputs , when deciding @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Downstream along Walnut Creek , even a few inches of lake drawdown can ease pressure on neighborhoods and roads that frequently flood . <h> A system built for a changing city <p> Raleigh 's growth has brought more pavement , rooftops and parking lots , which change where rain flows and how quickly it reaches creeks . At the same time , the region is seeing heavier downpours linked to a warming climate . <p> Marks said the model takes updated land-use and stormwater data into account . " As there is more urbanization or changes to the drainage system , the model updates with it , " she said . <p> The system does not forecast long-term climate trends , but the short-term forecasts adjust as storms become more intense . <h> People still make the decisions <p> Despite its use of artificial intelligence , the system does not release water or close roads automatically . It simply alerts staff when rainfall or water levels reach thresholds . <p> " The decision to release the water is a decision that people make , " Marks said . " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ City crews receive training on how to interpret the dashboard and run " what if " storm scenarios , which help them place barricades sooner and position resources more precisely . <h> A tool other cities are now watching <p> AEM says interest in this type of technology is growing , especially as flash floods increase nationwide . Raleigh is now in the fourth phase of building out its system and is planning to add more monitoring points next year . <p> Marks sees artificial intelligence playing a growing role , though never replacing people entirely . <p> " AI will continue to be important , " she said . " But it will never be the complete answer . You always need the human element . "

@@131647388 <h> The Climate Crisis Needs a New Catchphrase <h> " Two degrees " is n't cutting it . <p> Sign up for the Slatest to get the most insightful analysis , criticism , and advice out there , delivered to your inbox daily . <p> For half a century , scientists have been warning about the risk of the planet warming by " 2 degrees . " It 's a catchphrase that plagues the conversation about climate concerns , including at the United Nation 's COP30 meeting in Bel ? m , Brazil , this month . Take U.N . General Assembly President Annalena Baerbock 's remarks to the press this week , in which she stated that member countries had previously committed to limiting global warming " well below two degrees . " That 's a huge mistake . Well , the math is right . But the wording , at least where Americans are concerned , is dead wrong . <p> " Two degrees " is a benchmark in Celsius . And the world 's leader in per capita carbon emissions -- a leading culprit of the greenhouse @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Americans speak in Fahrenheit . Many folks are already loath to take action to combat climate change . Thanks to the rallying cry of " 2 degrees , " people in the U.S. are likely to mistake the dangerous warming of the planet as happening almost half as slowly . <p> Among U.N . member states , the U.S. is an outlier in sticking with the Fahrenheit scale . A few other smaller nations such as the Cayman Islands and Liberia , use it , too . But almost every other country in the world uses the Celsius system . Normally , I would n't suggest kowtowing to the Americans and their strange instance on measuring things their own way . But if a bit of temperature translation will help light a fire , so to speak , in the perpetrators , it 's worth it . <p> In some ways , the 2-degree communication debacle is a home-grown problem for the United States . It was 50 years ago , within its borders , that Yale University economics professor William Nordhaus started the conversation around this benchmark by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2 or 3 degrees Celsius " would take the climate outside of the range " that humans had been living in for millennia . The focus around 2 degrees gained traction and became a central " speed limit " for climate change . Back in 2015 , a report from the Carbon Brief noted that , " Limiting warming to no more than two degrees has become the de facto target for global climate policy . " That same year , a global treaty known as the Paris Agreement ( which the U.S. had signed on to and , under Trump , has withdrawn from ) set a target to keep global warming under a limit of 2 degrees . Nordhaus likely spoke in Celsius because it remains the temperature scale for researchers , regardless of where they are on Earth . This is similar to the way professional bakers , even in the States , measure in grams . People are willing to do those conversions to make sure their pastry does n't burn . They do n't seem willing to do the same for their planet . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Slate <p> A difference of 2 degrees Celsius is , depending on the exact temperature on the scale , equivalent to around 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit . That might sound like splitting hairs , but consider this : Climate warming is not linear . Each degree increase accelerates the problem . Take the example of measuring a child 's temperature . Let 's say it starts out at 39 degrees Celsius . That 's equal to 102.2 degrees Fahrenheit -- a true fever . But a " 2-degree " Celsius increase is n't equivalent to reaching 104.2 Fahrenheit ( still a fever , but manageable at home ) . Forty-one degrees Celsius equals 105.8 degrees Fahrenheit -- a medical emergency that would mean an immediate trip to the ER , at the very least , or a call for an ambulance . <p> Americans may not understand that scientists talking about a 2-degree difference in climate are speaking about what translates into more -- often around double the rise in number -- in Fahrenheit . And yet , even some prominent television and news coverage centers around the issue of 2 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Even NASA , a U.S. agency , has published a headline in Celsius ( an easy mistake for a science-focused institution to make ) . The Wikipedia page on the " 2 degree climate target " does n't , as of this writing , include a mention of a Fahrenheit equivalent . <p> Between 1970 and 2023 , the global average temperature already increased about 1.7 degrees Fahrenheit . We 're warned that at 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit warmer -- the equivalent of the famous 2-degree Celsius benchmark -- somewhere between 800 million to 3 billion people would face chronic water scarcity . And , unfortunately , the United Nations Environment Programme has stated that at the rate we 're going , we 're on track for a 5-degree Fahrenheit rise in average global temperatures by the end of the century . Perhaps no issue is more important than global warming when it comes to the future of the world and the lives our children will lead . If a conversion can help even a few more Americans understand it , it 's worth a shot . <p> I 'm not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ climate apathy . But a few small changes could help : Headlines in U.S. outlets should be in Fahrenheit . U.N . leaders need to go to greater lengths to translate their message into Fahrenheit , in addition to Celsius . To put it another way , they do n't need to go the extra kilometer to make sure we all know how dire things could become -- they need to go the extra mile .
